content: Actinobacteria, also known as Actinomycetes, are a group of Gram-positive bacteria characterized by a high guanine and cytosine (G+C) content in their DNA. These microorganisms are abundant in soil and play a critical role in the decomposition of organic materials, such as cellulose and chitin. Through this process, they contribute significantly to the turnover of organic matter and the carbon cycle, replenishing essential nutrients in the soil and aiding in the formation of humus. Actinobacteria are renowned for their ability to produce secondary metabolites, which makes them of great pharmacological and commercial interest. In 1940, Selman Waksman discovered that these soil bacteria produce actinomycin, a groundbreaking finding that earned him a Nobel Prize. Since then, hundreds of naturally occurring antibiotics have been identified from these microorganisms, particularly from the genus Streptomyces. In addition to their presence in soil, some Actinobacteria are found in association with plants and animals. While many are beneficial, a few species are pathogenic. Notable pathogenic genera include Mycobacterium, Corynebacterium, Nocardia, Rhodococcus, and certain species of Streptomyces. The genomes of 44 different strains of Actinobacteria, representing various genera, have either been sequenced or are currently undergoing sequencing. Some Actinobacteria form branching filaments that resemble the mycelia of fungi, which led to their initial classification alongside fungi under the older name Actinomycetes. However, they are unrelated to fungi. Most Actinobacteria are aerobic, but a few, such as Actinomyces israelii, are capable of growing under anaerobic conditions. Unlike the Firmicutes, another major group of Gram-positive bacteria, Actinobacteria have DNA with a high GC-content. Additionally, some species of Actinomycetes produce external spores. Representative genera of Actinobacteria include: Actinomyces Arthrobacter Corynebacterium Frankia Micrococcus Micromonospora Mycobacterium Nocardia Propionibacterium Streptomyces
